about.heading: About
about.ee_heading: What do we mean by ‘ethnic European’?
about.europhobia: Ethnic Europhobia is the precise term for antiwhite bias against people of ethnic European heritage. Official statistics and news coverage often use the broader label ‘White’, which can mix different groups together. Using this term keeps the claim specific and testable against the heritage data this project assembles.

term.ee_tip: Ethnic Europeans are people whose ancestry traces to the native peoples of Europe, often called ‘White’.

method.scale_intro: Each harm is scored out of 100. Heritage counts for most of the score. Full marks require separately identifying ethnic Europeans, not only a broader category such as White, or a proxy such as nationality. Heritage is 75 points and is awarded only when a published cross-table records the child victim's heritage and the offender's heritage for the same cases. One-sided data scores 0 for heritage.
method.cap_applied_body: The uncapped total is {uncapped}%. A country with no real ethnicity data is capped at 25%.
method.previous: On the previous rubric this country scored {score}%.
method.previous_with_band: On the previous rubric this country scored {score}% ({band}).
method.previous_weights: Harm weights changed on {date}. With the earlier weights (sexual abuse 25%, the other five harms 15% each) this country scored {score}%.
method.colours: Scored countries are shown in red on the map. The percentage in the text is the completeness score. Scores are reviewed as new data is found (last review {date}).
method.gold: 100% means a country publishes data that separately identifies ethnic Europeans, both as perpetrators (so one can tell when they disproportionately harm a group) and as child victims (so one can tell when ethnic European children are disproportionately harmed), alongside every other group, linked victim to perpetrator, for every harm. Heritage points require that link as a published cross-table for the same child cases. One-sided data scores 0 for heritage.
method.cap: Heritage points are awarded only for a published cross-table of child victim and offender heritage for the same cases. One-sided data scores 0 for heritage. Proxies such as nationality or migration background earn at most one quarter of the heritage points. A published “White” category that merges Hispanic people or another group, so ethnic Europeans cannot be isolated, is also scored as a proxy under the same cap. A country with no real ethnicity data is capped at 25%, however complete its other counting is.
method.weights: The country score is a weighted average of five harms: homicide 27.78%, sexual abuse 22.22%, sex trafficking 22.22%, physical abuse 16.67% and online exploitation 11.11% (weights in use since 24 November 2026). Neglect is not part of the score.
method.comp_victim_full: Published by harm, with ethnic Europeans identified separately — not only a broader category such as White, or a proxy such as nationality. These points are awarded only inside that paired child cross-table. One-sided victim data scores 0.
method.comp_perp_full: The same standard for perpetrators. These points are awarded only inside that paired child cross-table. One-sided perpetrator data scores 0.
method.comp_other_full: Broad coverage, a low share of unknowns, rates per 100,000, victim–perpetrator linkage, and public, timely release.

media.methods_cdi: The CDI is the calculation behind the Antiwhite media bias index. It is used in methods only, not as a second public name. CDI = (White-on-Black media count ÷ Black-on-White media count) ÷ (White-on-Black baseline count ÷ Black-on-White baseline count). 1 means coverage is proportional to the baseline; above 1 means White-on-Black stories are over-represented; below 1 means Black-on-White stories are over-represented. When a cell is 0, a point estimate is not published. The incident-based homicide audit is shown on this tab as a draft and is not a final finding. CDI remains a methods term only.

demographics.title: Demographic change, census first
demographics.lede: For countries that publish ethnicity, race, ancestry or migration-background census data, the score is the change in the founding population’s share since the baseline census. A negative figure means that share fell. Where a country publishes no ethnicity data, the same scale shows a UN migrant-origin proxy for 1990–2020. Census figures come first.

demographics.map_h: Which countries have seen declines in their founding populations?
demographics.map_desc: Dark green countries have growing founding populations; green have stable founding populations; light red have declining founding populations; medium red have strongly declining founding populations; dark red have very strongly declining founding populations.
demographics.legend_title: Percent change in founding population share since the baseline census
demographics.scale_note: Bands use the value as shown, and they do not overlap. These are not the Crime tab’s steps and not the UN dissimilarity index. The same colours are used for the UN proxy.
demographics.bar_desc: Census figures come first, on a signed scale of percent decline in the founding share (zero is marked). Where a country publishes no ethnicity data, the rows that follow are a UN migrant-origin proxy for the same percent decline, covering 1990–2020.
demographics.selected_census: Census: the percent change in the founding population’s share is {change}% (latest year {year}). A negative figure is a percent decline.
demographics.method_p1: When a country publishes ethnicity, race, ancestry or migration-background data that can be mapped to the founding pool, the score is the percent change in that pool’s share of the population, from the earliest comparable official figure to the latest: (latest share − first share) / first share × 100. A negative figure is a percent decline; a positive figure means the share rose.
demographics.method_p2: Most countries do not record ethnicity. For those countries the same scale shows a UN migrant-origin proxy. The founding share in a year is 100 minus the cross-pool foreign-born share, and the score is the percent change in that founding share from 1990 to 2020. The proxy counts first-generation migrant origin only and can understate change, because native-born descendants and native minorities stay in the founding pool. In Canada, the founding population’s share of ethnic Europeans fell by 28.9% from 1971 to 2021, while the UN proxy for the same percent change is −10.07% and the UN dissimilarity index D is 9.6. Proxy countries use the same colours as census countries and carry a small proxy tag.
demographics.method_p3: The primary pool is the historical majority, or the founding population of the modern state. Post-1970 migration is not a reason to change it; that migration is what the score measures. Aboriginal Australians are handled only for Australia and are not a separate pool. Horn of Africa groups sit in the Sub-Saharan African pool and are flagged as adjacent to the Semitic / Middle East and North Africa pool, which includes Arab, Middle Eastern, Persian and ethnic Jewish populations.
demographics.method_p4: Quality letters apply only to the UN estimates. Letter A means foreign-born (birthplace) data; B means citizenship-based data, or more than 20% of migrants of unknown origin; C means the series was imputed by UN DESA, or is citizenship-based and more than 20% unknown.
demographics.quality_b: B: citizenship-based data, or over 20% of migrants of unknown origin.
demographics.quality_c: C: imputed by UN DESA, or citizenship-based and over 20% unknown.
demographics.method_p5: The colour bands use the percent change as shown and do not overlap. Above +2% is dark green, −2% to +2% is green, −7% up to but not including −2% is light red, −15% up to but not including −7% is mid red, and below −15% is bright red. They are not the Crime tab’s steps and not the UN dissimilarity index. A grouping view shows whether a country has census ethnic data, an official series that cannot be turned into a cross-pool score, a UN proxy only, or no score. Areas on the not-scored list are grey and are left out of the ranked list. That list is every area with fewer than 100,000 people in 2024, except the Falkland Islands and the European micro-territories Faroe Islands, Isle of Man, Andorra, Liechtenstein, Monaco and San Marino, plus a named set. The Falkland Islands and those six stay scored, and a population under 100,000 is still flagged on a scored row. Australia and Israel have official series that cannot be mapped to a founding-pool score without inventing a mapping; they are shown with the UN proxy and labelled separately. This tab is not a published finding.
demographics.source_caption: Census scores: official statistical-office series compiled in the StopBias ethnic-pools global dataset v1.7.0. Fallback scores: UN DESA International Migrant Stock 2024. Founding pools and regions: country_pool_map.csv. World population shares: UN World Population Prospects 2024 (geographic, not ethnicity). Boundaries: Natural Earth 1:50m.
demographics.pool_MENA: Semitic / Middle East and North Africa
demographics.records_p1: Most countries do not record ethnicity, race or ancestry in their census. Without those records, the public cannot see how the ethnic composition of a country has changed.
demographics.records_p2: Counts of first-generation migrant origin miss later generations and understate change. In Canada, the founding population’s share of ethnic Europeans fell by 28.9% from 1971 to 2021, while the UN migrant-origin dissimilarity index is 9.6.
demographics.records_p3: Statistics offices are urged to publish accurate, comparable ethnic data so this change can be measured rather than hidden by incomplete records.
demographics.records_p4: The UN World Population Prospects (a geographic series, not an ethnicity series) show that Europe, Northern America and Oceania together were {first}% of world population in {first_year} and {latest}% in {latest_year}. That is a change in where people live, not a substitute for ethnic records.

demographics.tooltip_proxy: {score}%, 1990–2020. UN estimate: percent change in the founding share, where that share is 100 minus the share of residents born in another country whose origin differs from the country’s founding population (for example, someone born in India living in Canada). People born in the country are counted as founding population, so this is a lower bound; where both exist, the census percent decline is usually much larger (Canada: census −28.9% vs UN estimate −10.07%).
demographics.selected_proxy: {score}%, 1990–2020. UN estimate: percent change in the founding share, where that share is 100 minus the share of residents born in another country whose origin differs from the country’s founding population (for example, someone born in India living in Canada). People born in the country are counted as founding population, so this is a lower bound; where both exist, the census percent decline is usually much larger (Canada: census −28.9% vs UN estimate −10.07%).
